articles.title: How the Brewers and Rays got to baseball's biggest stage with small budgets and small ball

image.caption: The Milwaukee Brewers are getting ready to do battle with the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series. The best-of-seven Fall Classic begins Friday evening. (Ashley Landis/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

A new World Series champion will be crowned this year, as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy. Here's how they got there and what to expect.
Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, two of MLB's lowest-spending teams, have the chance to make history this season
A new World Series champion will be crowned as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy.
Neither franchise has won it all before, meaning it will be a history-making outcome no matter who wins the Fall Classic.

Ahead of the first game in the best-of-seven series on Friday, we're taking a look at how the Brew Crew and the D-Rays got here, the Canadian connections, their World Series records and what it means to see two teams with relatively small payrolls make it this far into the playoffs
Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates his team's Game 6 victory over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. (David J. Phillip/The Associated Press)
Comparatively puny payrolls
Milwaukee and Tampa are in the bottom-half of MLB's 30 franchises when it comes to payroll spending.

The Brewers had an Opening Day roster payroll of just over $124 million US — 19th in the majors according to The Associated Press. The Rays' payroll was just $88.7 million US, ranked 26th at that time.
Compare that to Toronto's Opening Day payroll of nearly $269 million US, the fifth-highest in baseball. And yet, the Jays missed the playoffs.
The deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers had a payroll of nearly $317 million US at the season's start. And while they made the playoffs, they got swept — by the Brewers.

items: Shorter regular season among drastic changes MLB proposes to players
Baseball labour talks have begun — here's what could be in store for the league and the Jays

blocks.text: None of this is helping the argument of the MLB owners, who are pushing for a salary cap to be established in the league, arguing that baseball's richest teams are too dominant. It's all part of negotiations taking place as baseball's current five-year deal expires in December.
The Associated Press says this year's World Series marks the first time since 1991 that two teams with payrolls in the bottom half of the majors will compete for the title.

Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers hits a home run in Game 3 of the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Bauers led his team with 26 homers during the regular season. (Kiyoshi Mio/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Homer drought
The Brewers were tied for the second-lowest, regular-season home-run total, with just 154 round-trippers. Only the Blue Jays hit fewer home runs (152).
Despite this power outage, Milwaukee put together a 103-59 season — the best in the game.
Tampa's lineup slugged 169 homers prior to the playoffs, which put them at 22nd in the majors. The Rays wrapped their regular season with a 98-64 record.
Toronto Blue Jays leave fans with little to cheer about
The power of 'small ball'

The strategy of small ball — getting runners on base and advancing them by stealing bases or putting the ball in play with sacrifice hits and bunts — was key for both Milwaukee and Tampa as they outplayed rivals in their respective leagues.
The Rays led the majors with 45 sacrifice bunts during the regular season. The Brewers had 37, the fifth-most overall.
The two teams also stole a ton of bases: The Rays swiped 164 bases prior to the playoffs, while Millwaukee claimed 162.

This year's World Series could be the first with a 104-mile-per-hour pitch, thanks to Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski. The 24-year-old threw a record 1,115 pitches of 100 miles per hour or higher in his first full major league season. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)
Triple-digit heat
The Brewers' ace starting pitcher, Jacob Misiorowski, is the most prolific, hard-throwing pitcher in the game.
He's thrown more than 1,100 pitches at speeds exceeding 100 miles per hour this season.

items: Surprising Rays-Brewers showdown to open Friday with Jacob Misiorowski's record heat

blocks.text: Misiorowski has already set the record for the fastest pitch thrown in a playoff game (104.8 miles per hour) — at least, since tracking started in 2008. Amazingly, that's not the hardest pitch he's ever thrown.
He's slated to start Game 1 for the Brewers on Friday night.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Freddy Peralta and catcher Liam Hicks celebrate after a strikeout in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians on Oct. 13. (Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)
Canadian catcher
Toronto-born ballplayer Liam Hicks joined the Rays at the trade deadline.
The 27-year-old catcher is in his second big-league season, joining Tampa in August, after first getting to the big leagues with the nearby Miami Marlins.

items: Liam Hicks spent teenage years in Toronto area before baseball career blossomed

blocks.text: So far this post-season, Hicks has six hits, one run, three walks and four RBIs across nine games he's played with the Rays.

Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash has served as the team's skipper for 12 seasons — including in 2020, when the Rays played in the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. (Kim Klement Neitzel/Imagn Images/Reuters)
The ex-Jays catcher
Rays manager Kevin Cash was a player before he was a manager and started out his major-league career in Toronto.
Cash appeared in 101 games for the Jays from 2002-2004. He later played for the Rays, the Boston Red Sox, the New York Yankees and the Houston Astros.
He's managed the Rays for 12 seasons, including in 2020 when Tampa lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
A long wait for Brewers fans
Milwaukee last made it to the World Series in 1982 — back when Ronald Reagan was in the White House, and years before any of the current Brewers players were born.
The Brewers lost in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Hall of Famer Robin Yount was part of the Milwaukee team that lost to St. Louis, and he recently said he'll "never get over it until the Brewers win one."
On Tampa's side, the Rays have been to the World Series twice, losing both times: First in 2008 and again in 2020.
Brewer Robin Yount plays in Game 4 of the 1982 World Series against the St. Louis Cardinals, which the Brewers went on to lose. (The Associated Press)
Where to watch
Canadian baseball fans can catch the World Series on Sportsnet.
Most games will air on the main Sportsnet channel — except for Games 2 and Game 7 (if necessary), which will run on Sportsnet One.
All games will also stream on Sportsnet+.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
articles.summary: She was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo.

blocks.text: Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.

The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.

Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] High barriers, high stakes: The SEC’s liquidity gambit
articles.summary: The Philippines needs to turn its moribund stock exchange into an engine for genuine capital formation

items: SEC Chairman Francis Lim's proposal to raise brokerage capital to P120 million aims to modernize the Philippine capital market but faces opposition from smaller brokerages, which fear consolidation or closure.
The Philippine Association of Securities Brokers and Dealers (PASBDI) argues for a tiered capital framework based on risk, highlighting that smaller firms can still pose significant systemic risks.

While the SEC's reforms are intended to enhance market resilience and investor trust, there are concerns about the operational impact of new requirements, such as a proposed P20 million surety bond, which could strain smaller firms financially.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

SEC Chairman Francis Lim’s push to raise brokerage capital and stand up market-making standards addresses decades of market stagnation. But as veteran broker Vivian Yuchengco warns that a uniform P120-million threshold threatens smaller Filipino houses, regulators must balance systemic resilience with competitive access.
The Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) drive to modernize the Philippine capital market has encountered organized resistance.

Veteran stockbroker Vivian Yuchengco, chair of the Philippine Association of Securities Brokers and Dealers (PASBDI), warns that the SEC’s proposed P120-million unimpaired paid-up capital (UPC) requirement could push smaller Filipino brokerage houses into forced consolidation or closure.
Though her warning carries economic weight, SEC Chairman Francis Lim’s regulatory rationale is compelling.

In an interview with Vantage Point, Yuchengco narrates that a firm operating at the current P30-million baseline would have to raise an additional P90 million—a fourfold increase. Yet the central question is whether preserving the industry’s historical headcount should take precedence over building robust safeguards for the investing public.

Philippine capital markets have drifted for decades in a low-liquidity trap, constrained by shallow trading depth, sluggish turnover, and governance structures that have shielded incumbents at the expense of dynamism.

Chairman Lim’s multi-pronged reform agenda—raising broker-dealer capitalization, placing term limits on long-tenured Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) broker-directors, and introducing rigorous market-making rules—is not mere routine oversight. (READ: [Vantage Point] SEC’s float gambit: Shaking the stock market from deep slumber)

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] PSE veterans take SEC term-limit fight to Court of Appeals

blocks.text: It is an urgent, necessary modernization drive designed to rebuild credibility, fortify market resilience, and turn the country’s moribund exchange into an engine for genuine capital formation.

Chairman Lim explains that modern brokerage operations require substantial financial stamina not just for trade execution, but for enterprise cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, risk management, and market development. Furthermore, decades of inflation have severely eroded the real purchasing power of historical capital baselines.

Crucially, two distinct initiatives must not be conflated. The general P120-million UPC rule is a draft proposal envisioned for phased rollout through 2030. By contrast, the P150-million threshold under SEC Memorandum Circular No. 28, Series of 2026, applies strictly to brokerages volunteering as designated market makers.

Because market makers continuously quote two-way prices, bridge supply-demand gaps, and hold securities on their own books, an elevated capital buffer is essential to withstand sharp volatility without sparking settlement contagion.

blocks.caption: [Market Rider] SEC’s market maker push and how it can boost PH stock trading

blocks.text: Still, PASBDI’s newly released 10-page position paper, “Calibrated Capital, Credible Protection,” introduces salient counterarguments.

In a survey of 55 brokerage firms, PASBDI found that 54.5% (30 firms) oppose the uniform P120-million rule, with another eight backing it only with revisions. Among 36 respondents relying on the P30-million threshold, 25 voiced opposition; conversely, none of the five firms already holding P120 million or more objected. While the survey does not capture the entire industry, it confirms that resistance is concentrated among smaller-capitalized houses.

PASBDI’s most persuasive point centers on regulatory proportionality. Invoking Principle 30 of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the association argues that prudential mandates should mirror the actual risks intermediaries assume.

It proposes a three-tiered capital framework, contending that a firm merely introducing clients to clearing brokers should not face the same regulatory burden as an institution carrying customer margin financing, holding custody of assets, or running heavy proprietary books.

This risk-based philosophy has merit. Yet smaller size does not automatically equate to lower risk. Even modest brokerages can inflict systemic reputational damage and catastrophic investor losses through deficient custody, lax internal controls, or operational misconduct. Any tiered model must never compromise the baseline safety of customer assets.
PASBDI also raises a valid operational objection to the proposed P20-million surety bond mandated for December 2028, ahead of the capital milestones in 2029 and 2030.

If underwriters require 100% collateral, the bond would immobilize liquid funds urgently needed for daily trading and settlement. A firm facing a P90-million equity call alongside a cash-collateralized P20-million bond would endure an effective P110-million immediate funding drain.
Consequently, PASBDI recommends stretching the glide path—proposing P60 million by 2029 and P90 million by 2032.
However, other association compromises prove less convincing. PASBDI suggests temporarily recognizing independently appraised increases in real estate owned by brokerages as regulatory capital.

Here, regulators must hold firm. Property valuations on paper cannot settle failed trades, satisfy immediate margin calls, or reimburse retail investors in a flash crash. Illiquid brick-and-mortar assets are no substitute for genuine, loss-absorbing liquidity.
Financial statements across the street underscore that capital size, profitability, and regulatory cushion must be evaluated separately.
Independent retail leader COL Financial held P1.78 billion in net liquid capital and an extraordinary 548.33% risk-based capital adequacy ratio (RBCA) as of June 2026.
Bank-backed BDO Securities absorbed a P189.71-million net loss in 2025, yet maintained P487.15 million in equity and P216.85 million in net liquid capital, remaining fully compliant.
First Metro Securities reported P169 million in paid-up capital, backed by documented operational experience running market-making for the First Metro ETF.
BPI Securities logged P202.36 million in capital despite an operating loss, while AB Capital posted P97.84 million in combined capital stock and APIC.

blocks.caption: Yuchengco tells SEC’s Lim: Fresh PSE blood is shareholders’ call

blocks.text: Meanwhile, traditional firms like David Go Securities—which closed 2025 with P42.45 million in unimpaired capital, P12.59 million in net profit, and a sound 199% RBCA ratio—prove that compliant, profitable houses could be locked out under a rigid, one-size-fits-all threshold.

PASBDI’s most constructive recommendation is for the SEC to publish a formal regulatory impact assessment detailing the risks addressed, the firms affected, and the competitive fallout. Doing so would fortify, not diminish, Lim’s authority.

As Chairman Lim told Vantage Point: “Our message is clear: market making must create real liquidity, not artificial activity; fair competition, not unfair advantage. The SEC’s rules require safeguards for conflicts of interest, transparent quotation standards, and accountable incentives. We want a market that is not only more active, but also fairer, more transparent, and worthy of investor trust.”
The same philosophy must anchor the broader capitalization reforms. Lim deserves strong support for tackling structural stagnation that has hobbled the exchange for decades.

The goal should not be to protect every legacy player regardless of capability, nor to arbitrarily purge viable independent firms. It is to forge an industry resilient enough to withstand shocks, expand market depth, and command public trust.

By taking legitimate proportionality concerns into account, the SEC can refine its timeline without diluting its mandate—ensuring that the investing public remains the ultimate beneficiary. – Rappler.com

Sources: PASBDI, Calibrated Capital, Credible Protection (October 2026); SEC draft amendments to Rules 28.1 and 33.1; SEC Memorandum Circular No. 28, Series of 2026; and audited brokerage financial statements filed with CMIC. Historical figures do not establish current SEC accreditation.

articles.title: When the Ifugao rice terraces rest
articles.summary: In Nagacadan, Kiangan, Ifugao, the rice terraces were not green when we came. They were resting, and that turned out to be one of the most important things to see.

blocks.text: IFUGAO, Philippines – Nagacadan was not wearing its postcard face when we arrived.

The terraces were not the bright green most visitors know from tourism posters. Some paddies were brown, others held shallow water, and several had already been cleared after harvest. For someone visiting Kiangan town for the first time, it was not quite the picture I had carried in my head.
But the longer we stayed, the more the landscape made sense.

Rice in Nagacadan is traditionally planted once a year. By October, much of the area is between harvest and the next planting cycle, with paddies resting or being prepared for planting again. What looked bare was not neglected land. It was farmland doing what farmland does.

blocks.caption: QUIET FIELDS. Nagacadan Rice Terraces in Kiangan, Ifugao, after harvest. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

blocks.text: We had come as part of the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan in the Cordilleras. Community guides led us down into the terraces, across streams and the river that cuts through the valley, and along narrow paths between paddies.

Nagacadan is one of the five clusters that make up the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras. Its form is striking from the ground, with two ascending rows of terraces facing each other across the river.

From a viewpoint, the terraces can look almost sculpted. Walking among them changes the scale. You begin to notice irrigation, soil, stone walls, paddies at different stages, houses, granaries, and the ordinary work needed to keep the whole system alive.
The terraces are not simply a view. They are farms.
One of the people walking with us was Johntrey “Dandan” Dinamling. He grew up around the landscape we had traveled to see, but that morning was also a first for him.

“I am Dandan Dinamling, and I am a local tour guide here in Nagacadan,” he told us in a mix of Filipino and English, nervous but smiling. “It was my first time to share my knowledge about our village.”
Dandan had also put school on hold. He stayed home to help with farming and, in the process, began learning how to guide visitors through a place he had known all his life.

He talked about the fields, heirloom rice, irrigation, traditional practices, and the need to preserve what remains. Sometimes he paused to search for a word. Sometimes people nearby helped him explain.
That did not make his story weaker. It made it more honest.
Dandan was not reciting a polished tourism spiel. He was trying to explain his own village to strangers, turning things familiar to him into something we could understand.
“I experienced farming,” he said simply, before talking about the rice, irrigation, and the work needed to keep the terraces productive.
For him, farming was not heritage in the abstract. It was work he had done with his own hands.

blocks.caption: SHARING. Johntrey Dinamling, a young local guide from Nagacadan, shares what he knows about the terraces, heirloom rice, irrigation and farming.

blocks.text: Now, guiding gives him another way to stay close to the land while helping outsiders understand why it matters. He spoke about wanting more visitors to come to Nagacadan, not simply for the scenery, but because tourism could also provide a livelihood and give people more reasons to stay connected to the community.

That matters in a place where the future of the terraces depends not only on conservation projects but also on people willing to keep farming, maintain irrigation, repair terrace walls, and pass on knowledge that cannot be learned from a brochure.
Dandan, in that sense, was part of the story of Nagacadan itself.
Before we entered an Ifugao house, our guides began singing. Those among us who knew the song joined in.
“Itetem ta humgopak.” (Put down the ladder so I can enter.)

Traditional Ifugao houses are raised above the ground and accessed by a wooden ladder that can be removed. In the song, the request to lower it conveys the feeling of someone coming home after a long journey, asking to be let in, to rest, and to be welcomed. Then we climbed.

blocks.caption: TRADITIONAL HOUSE. A traditional Ifugao house in Nagacadan, raised above the ground and built around a way of life shaped by farming, family and community. Inside are reminders that heritage is not just something displayed but something lived.

blocks.text: Nearby stood a traditional rice granary, another reminder of how deeply rice runs through life here. It is not only a crop. It has shaped work, storage, food, ritual, architecture, and the rhythm of the year.
The song stayed with me because it made the place feel less like a heritage site and more like what it has always been: home.
The night before, Kiangan Mayor Raldis Andrei Bulayungan had given us his own explanation of local hospitality.
“We don’t simply say welcome,” he said. “We also ask, ‘Have you eaten?’”
Even if visitors say they are already full, he joked, someone will probably insist that they eat again.
He urged us to try bakkle, a local rice cake wrapped in banana leaves, and suggested that calories consumed while appreciating culture should count as cultural education.

blocks.caption: RICE CAKE. Bakkle, a traditional Ifugao rice cake wrapped in banana leaves, in Kiangan. Simple, filling, and very much part of the welcome.

blocks.text: The laughter was easy, but his larger point was serious.
Tourism, Bulayungan said, should not be only about “visiting beautiful places or taking photographs.”
“It is about connecting with people, understanding their stories, appreciating their traditions, and creating friendships and memories that will last a lifetime,” he said.

Visitors also mean income for homestays, guides, food producers, performers, and other small businesses in Kiangan. For a town that wants more people to visit without losing what makes it unique, that balance matters.
There is a habit in travel of wanting places at their prettiest.
We want the terraces green, the skies clear, and everything timed perfectly for the camera.

Farming does not work that way. There is planting, growing, ripening, harvesting, clearing, preparation, and rest. A rice terrace is not failing when it turns brown. It is simply at another stage in the cycle.
Along the trail, I also saw gumamela (hibiscus) growing beside the path.
That took me straight back to childhood, when we used to crush the flowers and leaves, mix them with water, and make bubbles from the sticky liquid.
You can travel to a UNESCO World Heritage Site expecting something grand, only to be ambushed by a flower you played with as a child.
That may be one of the reasons Nagacadan stayed with me. It was not because it looked exactly as I expected, but because it did not.

By the time we climbed out, the terraces no longer felt like a landscape, which I had come to check off a list. They had become a working place shaped by farmers, guides, families, water, soil, memory, and time.
The green will return, and the rice will grow again. For now, Nagacadan is between seasons.
And the land, like the people who depend on it, knows when it is time to work and when it is time to rest. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia
articles.summary:
Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday

  • Get our
articles.byline: Adeshola Ore with Australian Associated Press

blocks.text: Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.
The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.
“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.
The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.
“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.
This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.
“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.
The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.
On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.
Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.
The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

articles.title: Canadian cybersecurity exec arrested by FBI accused of working with criminals to defraud his own clients
articles.summary: A Toronto-area cybersecurity executive arrested by the FBI amid a high-profile hacking probe colluded with cybercriminals to extort money from his own clients, according to U.S. prosecutors. The…

image.caption: Canadian cybersecurity expert Edward Dubrovsky was charged earlier this month in a U.S. federal court with an extortion conspiracy offence and "interference with commerce by threats," according to a public docket. (Ed Dubrovsky/LinkedIn)

blocks.text: World·New

A Toronto-area cybersecurity executive arrested by the FBI amid a high-profile hacking probe colluded with cybercriminals to extort money from his own clients, according to U.S. prosecutors. The explosive allegations laid out in a U.S. court provide a clearer indication of how Edward Dubrovsky is suspected of being involved with "threat actors" linked to the ShinyHunters cyber-gang.
Edward Dubrovsky arrested earlier this month in Philadelphia amid FBI probe focused on ShinyHunters cyber-gang
A Toronto-area cybersecurity executive arrested by the FBI amid a high-profile hacking probe colluded with cybercriminals to extort money from his own clients, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The explosive allegations laid out in a U.S. court provide a clearer indication of how Edward Dubrovsky is suspected of being involved with "threat actors" linked to the notorious ShinyHunters cyber-gang.

ShinyHunters claimed responsibility last month for hacking an FBI jobs portal and stealing a massive trove of data. The group typically demands ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it's obtained.

"The defendant was actually working on behalf of the threat actors," assistant U.S. attorney Anthony Carissimi claimed before a federal magistrate judge in Philadelphia on Oct. 8, according to a court transcript obtained by CBC News.
"Given that those are the charges and that is what he's been arrested for, I suspect that his business will dry up," the federal prosecutor added.
Dubrovsky will contest the charges, his court-appointed defence said.

items: Shock and surprise after FBI arrests Canadian cybersecurity expert in ShinyHunters hacking case

blocks.text: Dubrovsky, 54, was detained earlier this month during a trip to Philadelphia for a cybersecurity conference. He was charged with an extortion conspiracy offence and "interference with commerce by threats," according to a public docket.
At the time, FBI director Kash Patel said the agency had arrested a "suspected co-conspirator" of ShinyHunters. The RCMP said it was aware a Canadian had been arrested in connection with the case.

FBI director Kash Patel confirmed on Oct. 9 the agency had in recent days 'arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group,' the notorious cyber-gang linked to a hack targeting an FBI jobs portal. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

During Dubrovsky's 14-minute initial hearing in U.S. District Court, the federal prosecutor provided a brief overview of the case against the Canadian. He did not directly reference ShinyHunters or the FBI cyberattack.
"The reason [Dubrovsky] is sitting here is because he was engaging in essentially a fraud involving his own clients, his own business partners," Carissimi said.
He said Dubrovsky was "clearly engaged in cryptocurrency exchanges with, among other people, a criminal element."

Carissimi told the court that Dubrovsky had been dealing in the cryptocurrency Monero, which the prosecutor said is "renowned for being untraceable." He told the court that, while Dubrovsky has a Canadian passport, he's originally from Latvia and at one point also held an Israeli passport.
Tim Wright, a court-appointed federal defender, described the allegations against Dubrovsky as "completely untested."
"He wants to fight this to clear his name because of his reputation, because he's a businessman," Wright said.

Canadian firm CyberSteward shared this picture of Edward Dubrovsky signing copies of his book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia on Oct. 6. (CyberSteward/LinkedIn)
Self-described 'globally recognized' expert

On his LinkedIn profile, Dubrovsky describes himself as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert" who helps clients negotiate with ransomware attackers. He recently published the book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response, intended for victimized companies.
The day before his arrest, Toronto-based tech firm CyberSteward posted a picture of Dubrovsky signing copies of his new book at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia.

Heather Osborne, NetDiligence's director of global events and programming, told CBC News in an email that "to our knowledge," Dubrovsky's arrest "did not occur at our event, which ended at 11:30 a.m. on Oct 7."
CyberSteward has not responded to multiple requests for comment on the firm's ties to Dubrovsky, and his employment status.
Wright, the defence lawyer, said in court that Dubrovsky had planned to attend another conference in Canada on Oct. 15, then return to the U.S. for an event in South Carolina.
"He is a very well known and well respected businessman in cybersecurity," Wright said.
The FBI's criminal complaint remains under seal. The document would typically contain further details of the agency's investigation into a defendant and specifics of any alleged offence.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Scott W. Reid ordered Dubrovsky held in custody until he is transported to Texas, where the charges were filed and where he will appear for a formal detention hearing.
As of Friday, public records from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons showed Dubrovsky was still being held at the Philadelphia detention centre where he was taken on Oct. 7.
Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested in connection to FBI hacking case
'Every system' is vulnerable, Dubrovsky once told CBC
Dubrovsky previously served as managing director at CYPFER, the firm tasked with helping the city of Hamilton, Ont., recover from a 2024 cyberattack.
The company recently told CBC News that Dubrovsky wasn't involved in the Hamilton file.

items: Cybersecurity firm hired by Hamilton says director arrested by FBI didn't handle city's ransomware response

blocks.text: Once hired as a York University cybersecurity instructor, he appeared in Canadian media as a commentator on related issues and was previously interviewed by CBC News.
"Every organization uses vendors and service providers to do some of their business," Dubrovsky said in 2018, "so every single system in the world has vulnerabilities."

David Shipley, CEO of the Fredericton-based firm Beauceron Security, told CBC News in an interview earlier this month that Dubrovsky's case highlights his own longstanding reservations surrounding ransomware negotiators.
"We have seen people fall from grace before," Shipley recalled.
He urged ransomware victims who have backed up their data to seek to restore uninfected files, rather than paying a ransom.
"There's no guarantee that paying [the attackers] gets you out of the pain," he said.
If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.
With files from Kevin Maimann, Jeffery Tram, Aaron Saltzman and Reuters

articles.title: Are California voters about to impose world's first 'tax on billionaires'?
articles.summary: Voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
BySareen Habeshian
Reporting fromLos Angeles
Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions and being home to many rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide if the mega-rich among them - names that include media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.
Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".
But the vote is also offering regular everyday residents a voice on an issue that has riled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country - and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the whole of the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the globe. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she told the BBC.

blocks.caption: A "Yes to 40 This Lawn Is Watered By Billionaire Tears" yard sign among merchandise for sale during a "Yes on 40 for Ballots Over Billionaires" rally in San Francisco, California, US, on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.
The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries – Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue, she said.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly  given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

blocks.text: Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100 million to a political nonprofit funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.
They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.
Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he added, saying the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax. To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

blocks.caption: Chart of California billionaire's wealth

blocks.text: Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believes the way the measure is written is "problematic", it is necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.
Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief executive said in an interview with the BBC's news partner in the US, CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."
Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.
While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th century, that they have a God-given right to rule".
"They have all the wealth; they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on Nov 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson".

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.
Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment that is behind a policy" like Prop 40.
"This is really not about Prop 40," he says. It's about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

blocks.caption: Image caption, US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.

blocks.text: US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter speaks out for first time: ‘I have to go in’
articles.summary:
Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher

The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school…

blocks.text: The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last week spoke for the first time about the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.”
Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter, has received national attention and praise for stopping the bloodshed at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school.

He fatally shot Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school, who broke in and shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.

In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB), his first since the 15 October shooting, he recounted that day. He told reporters that he was only in the area because he had decided to return home and eat lunch with his wife rather than the meal he brought to work that day.

For a moment, Giamanco, who lives near the school, thought it was a prank when he saw a man in black armed with a gun headed toward Silver Rail, he said. Then he saw the man fire the gun and climb over a school fence. Giamanco pulled out a .40 caliber handgun from his center console and headed into the school parking lot, calling 911, before himself hopping over a fence to pursue the shooter.
He quietly followed Griffin without the teenager seeing him, at one point crawling on his hands and knees when he heard “children pleading for their lives”.
“I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,” he told OPB.

Giamanco crawled through a broken window and toward the special education class Griffin had entered, where a teacher was fighting with the shooter. He came into the classroom and fired his gun. Griffin fell and was reaching for his weapon before Giamanco, who said he “was afraid of him shooting anybody else”, shot him two more times.
He told OPB that he lies awake at night thinking of what he saw that day and the teenage perpetrator, and wonders if he could have done more.
“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told the outlet. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”
Giamanco said he wants to see safer schools with school resource officers at every site, and that he would like to raise funding to support school safety efforts.

articles.title: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
articles.summary: Younger Limoges residents see the destruction of their town hall as unfortunate collateral damage in a wider movement. For others, the fire was an unacceptable tragedy.

blocks.text: For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.
In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.
Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.
I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with €500,000 (£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?
"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.
Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."
She complains of having to live on €300 per month.
"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.
This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.
In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.
"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."
Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.
"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.
Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.
"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.
Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.
With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.
Additional reporting by Paul Pradier.

articles.title: Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
articles.summary: The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests to form the biggest challenge to Vučić's rule.

blocks.text: Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

articles.title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom
articles.summary:
BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say

The

blocks.text: The David Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.

Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.

Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.

The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.

She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”
But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.

For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”
Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.

blocks.caption: The hit BBC series returns with cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed ‘stonefish’. Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose Branco

blocks.text: That includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.

Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.

Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence.

Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. Episodes show how the climatecrisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.
Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.
White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”

Asked if the BBC’s £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.

items: Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer

articles.title: Chiefs, Opposition call for Alberta government to drop appeal of decision that quashed separation petition
articles.summary: With the Alberta referendum now in the books, some First Nation chiefs are calling on the provincial government to drop its appeal of a judge’s decision to quash the citizen petition on separation.

image.caption: Chief Allan Adam speaks in March outside of the Alberta legislature, calling on the province to stomp out the citizen petition on separation. With the referendum now done, Adam says the province should drop its appeal of a ruling on the petition. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
With the Alberta referendum now in the books, some First Nation chiefs are calling on the provincial government to drop its appeal of a judge’s decision to quash the citizen petition on separation.
Province says it won't be doing that

“I mean, now that the referendum’s happened, the issue’s moot,” said Siksika Nation Chief Samuel Crowfoot. “[Premier Danielle Smith] said up and down that she's not going to pursue another referendum. Well, I think now’s the chance for her to put action to those words and to drop that appeal.”
Crowfoot says doing so could help repair the relationship between First Nations and the province — a relationship, he says, right now is “fractured.”

"The people said it straight out: we are not going to go through a separation. So my question would be is: why hang on to a process that the Alberta people gave her no mandate to speak on?" Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation Chief Allan Adam said.

At issue is a petition led by pro-independence group Stay Free Alberta to prompt the province to consider a referendum question on separation. It garnered more than 300,000 signatures earlier this year.

items: First Nation chief seeks formal explanation after ballot shortages in Alberta referendum

blocks.text: NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi echoed the chiefs' calls at a news conference Friday morning.
“Certainly the First Nations are spending money on lawyers, we taxpayers are spending money on lawyers, let’s listen to what Albertans said on Monday and just drop it,” Nenshi said.
The province, however, says it won't be doing that. Justice Minister Mickey Amery said in a statement the government believes the "decision contained errors of law."
"Citizens should not have to meet a duty to consult to gather signatures from fellow citizens on a citizen initiative petition," Amery said.
The legal picture so far
Four First Nations — Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation, Siksika Nation, Blood Tribe and Piikani Nation — challenged the process involving Stay Free Alberta’s citizen petition.

items: Judge overturns Elections Alberta’s approval of separation referendum petition

blocks.text: In May, Justice Shaina Leonard ruled that there had been a failure to consult with the First Nations, and she overturned Elections Alberta’s approval of the petition.

Because of that ruling, the government’s question on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot asked if Albertans supported the province starting the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.
The government launched an appeal of Leonard’s decision. Mitch Sylvestre, who led the petition drive, is also appealing it.
Crowfoot said he does not expect Sylvestre to drop his appeal.
“So, we’ll handle Mitch’s, but Danielle should drop hers on the part of the government of Alberta,” he said.
Mitch Sylvestre hold boxes of signatures before submitting them for a separation referendum to Elections Alberta in Edmonton on May 4, 2026. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)
For his part, Sylvestre says he would like to see the government continue its appeal.
“I think, moving forward for democracy here in Alberta, it's very important that they have to appeal that,” Sylvestre said.

“Because, I mean, this is a very contentious question, but there's gonna be other questions that somebody's going to disagree with. And, you know, all of a sudden, I can see that it won't be long they won't be able to ask any questions.”
According to unofficial results, Albertans voted 75 per cent in favour of the province remaining a part of Canada.
What could happen next?
Because there are two appeals, the process would continue regardless if the government dropped its appeal, said Kathleen Mahoney, professor emeritus at the University of Calgary's faculty of law.
Continuing its appeal could also give the government more clarity going forward, she said.
“They may want to know exactly when in a government process that affects Indigenous rights a consultation has to take place,” she said.
Constitutional experts have told CBC News that if an appeal is granted, the petition could indeed move forward.

“If the [appeal] court agrees with the court below, it's over,” Mahoney said. “But if the court decides that the consultation could have taken place later in the process, well, then we're into a different scenario.”
In the latter case, it would trigger a requirement for the government to deal with the initial citizen petition, she said, but there is no timeline set for when that would need to happen.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca

articles.title: Group files Competition Bureau complaint over Israeli real estate events in Toronto, Montreal
articles.summary: A group of lawyers and civil society members have filed a complaint with the Competition Bureau over Israeli real estate events in Toronto and Montreal, alleging that illegal properties were marketed…

image.caption: A general view of the West Bank Jewish settlement of Efrat. Canada and much of the international community have long held that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal and an obstacle to peace in the Middle East. (Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo)

blocks.text: A group of lawyers and civil society members have filed a complaint with the Competition Bureau over Israeli real estate events in Toronto and Montreal, alleging that illegal properties were marketed to Canadians under false pretences.

The complaint alleges at least four Israeli real estate companies and one Canadian marketing firm promoted properties in occupied Palestinian territories in the West Bank while misleading consumers to believe they were in Israel.

The Competition Bureau says it will review the complaint filed by Global Echo Litigation Center and the Canadian Lawyers for International Human Rights and determine if an investigation into the companies is warranted.

James Yap, president of the lawyers' association and a Windsor university law professor, said Canadians who may have purchased West Bank properties could be opening themselves up to serious legal consequences under international law, such as complicity in war crimes.

items: Canadian charities complicit in helping fund Israeli settlement movement in West Bank, critics say

blocks.text: Canada and much of the international community have long held that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal and an obstacle to peace in the Middle East.

The territory has been occupied by Israel since 1967, but settlement activity has significantly increased since the onset of the latest war in the Gaza Strip, triggered by the 2023 Hamas attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced most of Gaza's two million residents.
Ottawa advised Canadian businesses in August to avoid engaging with Israeli settlements, warning that failing to do so could open them up to legal and financial risk.

"The Canadian government talks a lot about upholding international law," Yap said. "We have our prime minister bemoaning the deterioration of the international rules-based order. They condemn the settlements as illegal. They talk about taking steps, taking action. This is a chance for the Canadian government to actually take action."
Complaint references photos, promo materials

The complaint, filed on behalf of six Canadians, compiles photos, social media posts and promotional materials of condo projects in the occupied West Bank being marketed at various real estate events from 2024 to 2026.

One photo of an Israeli real estate company's booth at the 2024 Great Israeli Real Estate Event in Montreal suggests the company promoted condo projects in Ma'ale Adumim and Adam, two Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside Israeli real estate.

items: Israel moving ahead with settlement plans that would split West Bank in two, rights group says

blocks.text: The company's booth advertised the developments with the message of finding one's "dream home in Israel."

Another company's booth at the same 2024 event advertised it as "your real estate agency in Jerusalem" while listing the locations of four Israeli settlements in the West Bank and two Israeli cities. The company is more explicit on its website, stating that its homes in West Bank settlements in Efrat, Mitzpe Yericho and Ma'ale Adumim are in Israel.

A Canadian marketing firm that helps North Americans buy Israeli real estate similarly lists a West Bank condo development as being in Israel on its website but it used more ambiguous language at a real estate event in Toronto.

The firm promoted a condo project in the Givat HaMatos settlement, located in East Jerusalem in the occupied West Bank, at the 2026 Israel Real Estate Briefing in Toronto with the tagline "own a piece of Jerusalem."
The lawyers behind the complaint to the Competition Bureau argue the ambiguity isn't enough to absolve the companies.

Under Canadian law, courts use a "general impression" test to determine if an advertisement is false or misleading. If an ad is literally true but omits essential information that would influence a consumer's behaviour, it could violate the Competition Act.

The lawyers argue that by promoting these properties at events titled the Great Israeli Real Estate Event and the Israeli Real Estate Briefing, and omitting mention of their true location in internationally-contested territories, the real estate companies misled Canadians.

Ariel Katz, a competition law expert who reviewed the complaint but was not involved in its filing, said he finds the evidence compelling, but couldn't say if the Competition Bureau would be likely to launch an inquiry.
"This is a highly politically charged topic, right? So whatever decision they make, they might be under enormous pressure," Katz said.

items: Pro-Palestinian supporters decry real estate events at synagogues over allegations occupied land being sold
Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, American journalist during West Bank olive harvest

blocks.text: Israel contends that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are not illegal because of Jewish people's historic connection to the land.

While the complaint deals with allegations of false advertising, Katz said the West Bank properties that were allegedly promoted at the events are considered illegal under international law, and Ottawa could ban the marketing of such properties altogether.
The lawyers behind the complaint say they're leaving the door open for future legal action that could target the illegality of the properties themselves.
Settler attacks on Palestinians communities rising: UN

The Canadian Press asked Global Affairs Canada if the sale of West Bank property is illegal in Canada and whether Canadians could be legally liable if they purchased such property but did not receive an answer before publication.

Emily Schaeffer Omer-Man, founder of Global Echo Litigation Center, said her law firm has been monitoring a "circuit" of Israeli real estate events in the United States, United Kingdom, France and other countries.
She said the complaint before the Competition Bureau gives Canada a chance to "pave the way" for other countries to follow suit in cracking down on these kinds of sales.

Marlee Wasser, one of the complainants, said she's a granddaughter of Holocaust survivors and sees the sale of Israeli settlement property in Canada as normalizing genocide in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians.
She added that protests outside Israeli real estate events have been used to justify restricting peoples' right to protest in Canada.
Documenting settler violence in the West Bank

The mayor of Vaughan, Ont., proposed a bubble zone bylaw — which ultimately passed — restricting protests near places of worship, schools and hospitals shortly after protesters demonstrated outside a local synagogue where an Israeli real estate event was being held in 2024.

For Basel Adra, an Oscar award-winning documentarian and community engagement manager at Global Echo Litigation Center, the complaint before the Competition Bureau is a chance for Canada to do "what's right."

The Palestinian filmmaker of "No Other Land," a documentary about the destruction of a West Bank community, says there's daily construction in the West Bank, building homes and roads for Israeli settlers.

items: Toronto city council passes controversial 'bubble zone' protest bylaw
Behind all the headlines about No Other Land

blocks.text: While he's never personally seen a Canadian settler in the West Bank, Adra said there are settlers from all over the world, especially America, in Israeli communities in the region.
Adra said he's been attacked by settlers several times, and last week a group of settlers invaded his family's land and cut down olive trees.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in June there was an average of six settler attacks on Palestinian communities in the West Bank each day of 2026 thus far that caused casualties or property damage, higher than any other year on record.

articles.title: Calgary family finds box of Pokémon cards valued at roughly $48,000
articles.summary: A Calgary family is giving thanks after they discovered an old box of Pokémon cards worth roughly $48,000 during Thanksgiving dinner.

image.caption: A forgotten batch of Pokémon cards has netted a Calgary family roughly $48,000 after they sold the box to a collectibles business in California. (submitted by Kirk Ledene)

blocks.text: Calgary
A Calgary family is giving thanks after they discovered an old box of Pokémon cards worth roughly $48,000 during Thanksgiving dinner.
'It felt like a little bit of an answered prayer,' said Colleen Ledene
Kirk Ledene was visiting his parents on the holiday when his mother asked him to go through some of his old boxes left in the basement.
He went down and found an old wooden box he'd made in shop class. Inside were some old hockey trophies as well as items he'd purchased at an auction house he worked at in the early 2000s.
And buried amongst the long-neglected items was an unopened box of Pokémon cards.
He brought the finds upstairs to show his kids.
“I showed the trophies off to the kids, and their jaws dropped when they saw the box in my hand,” said Kirk.
An initial search online revealed the box in question — a Wizards of the Coast Night booster box from 1999 — could be worth tens of thousands of dollars.
“It basically became like a piece of China, like don't touch it, don't breathe on it,” said Kirk.
Colleen Ledene, Kirk’s wife, was skeptical at first. “The only thing we talked about at Thanksgiving dinner was this stupid box,” she said. “At first I was like, this is really silly."
But she slowly started to realize it was actually a life-changing find.
A Calgary couple found a box of Pokémon cards worth roughly $48,000 while sorting through old boxes over Thanksgiving. (Underwood/CBC)
Online world of collecting
Next, the family dove into the online world of collectible cards, something that was entirely foreign to them.
They first reached out to auction houses and started to receive messages from interested buyers via social media after their son made a TikTok about the discovery.

After a lot of messaging and searching across social media platforms the couple found a collectibles dealer in Los Angeles — Edward Heikali, who runs E&A Collectibles. Since starting the business in 2020, he has focused on sealed vintage items, just like the box of Pokémon cards the Ledenes found.
“The value of it now is somewhere around the $40,000 US range and it's been steadily going up,” said Heikali.
The value of such boxes is dictated by basic supply and demand and the possibility that the cards within are themselves valuable, said Heikali.
He says stories like the Ledenes' happen quite often.
“A lot of the business that we do is helping people like Colleen that find these things and they then find us,” said Heikali.
For the Ledenes, choosing a buyer and deciding whether to ship or travel with the box to make the sale was a lot to think about.
“There's so many, like, logistical things and you know, like, customs or tariffs and stuff you don't know about or you have to think about,” said Kirk.
In the end they felt comfortable with Heikali and agreed to ship him the box via UPS.
“We just trusted this guy a lot,” said Kirk. "He would send all the forms that would be needed at customs so that just kind of relaxed both of us, making us know that he's done this a few times.”
The fact that Heikali operates a business and is not just an individual buyer also put their minds at ease.
Timing could not be better
The box has now been shipped and the Ledenes are anxiously awaiting the wire transfer.
Heikali says he'll look to sell the box to a collector or another business.
“It'll likely go to someone who's going to open it himself or to a business that is going to open it on behalf of their customers,” said Heikali.
For Kirk and Colleen, the timing of the discovery couldn’t be better.
"It felt like a little bit of an answered prayer ... just with everything going on in our life right now," Colleen said.

They don't know exactly what they'll do with the windfall, but a down payment on a new house, a family trip, and a dinner out with the folks — to thank them for not throwing out the box years ago — are all in the cards.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Bradley van Paridon is a Calgary based journalist. He can be reached at bradley.van.paridon@cbc.ca
